You are totally correct! Most of microeconomics is, by consensus and research, proven. There is little to argue about unless it is a very niche topic or a budding industry/model/framework. Macroeconomics, on the other hand, may not ever be truly "solved". First we had the Solow model, which assumed investors saved at constant rate and it was exogenously determined (meaning they did not decide for themselves). Then Ramsey-Cass-Koopmans came along and decided to let investors decide how much to save. The coolest part about these to models? They get the SAME ANSWER!

That is what I find awesome about macroeconomics. There are always new ways to design an economy, and many times there are unexpected results.

It does make sense. To add, even when the Phillips Curve was initially found, it turned out to be working only in the short run.

There's really just more to macroeconomics.

I really like the work of Minsky for this reason. He shows how different theories (e.g. Keynes vs. Hayek) come from different assumptions and effect the economy in different ways. They are not mutually exclusive ideas, in his mind. They are just fundamentally different situations.

If you are looking for a particular problem, the most cited, in my experience, is the "Equity Premium Puzzle."

Essentially, the argument questions why the long term rate of return on stock market investment is much higher than the return on government bonds. Traditional economic models predict that arbitrage opportunities will shift all rates of return to a similar rate of return - something that doesn't show up with real world empirical testing.

tl;dr: Are people really THAT risk averse they choose long term government bonds over stock market investing, even when it is common knowledge that investment in the stock market is mathematically more rewarding?
